strengths: Insightful probing analysis: Demonstrating that self-supervised speech (SS) representations—specifically layer 6 of HuBERT-base—linearly correlate strongly (r = 0.85) with EMG muscle action potential power provides a compelling mechanistic explanation for why intermediate SS layers excel at speech representation.

Geometric grounding of EMG features: The analysis of symmetric positive definite (SPD) covariance matrices and EMG power vectors D(E) across 13 distinct orofacial gestures provides sound evidence that EMG signals naturally form separable clusters reflecting articulatory mechanisms.

Dataset contribution: The collection of a ~9-hour EMG corpus spanning ~6,800 unique words at natural conversational speaking rates (115 wpm) is a substantial improvement over existing highly restricted, small-vocabulary neural interface benchmarks.
weaknesses: Incomplete speech synthesis evaluation: Despite the title and stated goal of direct EMG-to-speech synthesis, the paper does not evaluate the synthesized audio. Standard objective metrics (e.g., Mel-cepstral distortion, PESQ, STOI, or ASR-based Word/Character Error Rates on synthesized audio) and subjective listening tests (e.g., MOS) are completely missing. Section 6 explicitly states that evaluating perceptual quality, WER, and CER is 'Continuing work'.

High unit and phoneme error rates: The reported unit error rate (UER = 58.7%) and phoneme error rate (PER = 41.42%) are substantial. Without audio-level evaluations, it remains unproven whether the downstream Tacotron vocoder can produce intelligible or natural speech from such noisy discrete unit predictions.

Ambiguity regarding speaker diversity: While Section 5.1 tests 12 subjects on isolated orofacial gestures, Section 3 suggests the 9-hour continuous speech corpus was collected from only a single participant ('the subject'). The paper needs to explicitly clarify dataset demographics and discuss inter-subject variability/generalization.

Premature manuscript structure: The manuscript abruptly ends with Section 6 ('Continuing work') without an in-depth discussion, error analysis, or conclusion, giving the impression of an unfinished submission.

strengths: Interesting and insightful analysis exploring the linear relationship between self-supervised speech representations (e.g., HuBERT layer 6) and surface EMG power/articulatory gestures.
Substantial data collection effort consisting of approximately 9 hours of EMG data across an extensive vocabulary (~6,800 unique words) articulated at a natural speaking rate.
Formulating the EMG-to-speech mapping via discrete self-supervised units trained with CTC provides an appealing, alignment-free alternative to traditional vocoder regression pipelines.
weaknesses: Incomplete evaluation of the central claim: Despite the paper's title and premise ('synthesizing speech from electromyography'), there is no evaluation of the synthesized audio itself (e.g., PESQ, STOI, MCD, human MOS, or downstream ASR Word Error Rate). Section 6 explicitly states that developing models to assess perceptual quality and compute WER/CER is ongoing work.

High error rates: The reported unit error rate (58.7% UER) and phoneme error rate (41.42% PER) on greedy decoding are quite high, making it unclear whether the resulting Tacotron vocoder outputs produce intelligible or natural speech.

Lack of comparison with established EMG-to-speech baselines: The paper does not benchmark against existing open EMG-to-speech architectures or established approaches (such as Gaddy & Klein, 2020/2021) on either the proposed dataset or standard public benchmarks.

The speech dataset appears to be recorded from only a single participant ('with the subject articulating at a normal speaking rate'), which substantially limits claims regarding generalization and robustness across subjects.

strengths: Compelling scientific investigation into whether self-supervised speech representations (e.g., HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, WavLM) linearly align with articulatory muscle power derived from electromyography (EMG).

Insightful probing analysis across transformer layers, providing an articulatory interpretation for why intermediate layers (specifically layer 6 of HuBERT-Base) perform effectively in speech modeling tasks.
Effort to construct and open-source a natural-pace, large-vocabulary (6,800+ words, ~9 hours) EMG speech recording corpus.
weaknesses: The core claim and title of the paper ('synthesizing speech from electromyography') are not actually evaluated. The manuscript contains zero objective (WER, CER, MCD, STOI, PESQ) or subjective (MOS, intelligibility) evaluations of synthesized audio waveforms, with Section 6 explicitly confirming that assessing audio quality and computing WER/CER remains 'continuing work'.

Decoding error rates for the proposed pipeline remain very high (58.7% unit error rate and 41.4% phoneme error rate). Without speech intelligibility or perceptual metrics, it is impossible to determine whether the resulting synthesis is intelligible or usable.
Lack of empirical comparisons against established EMG-to-speech or silent-speech baselines from prior literature (e.g., Gaddy & Klein 2020/2021, Diener et al.).

Imprecision in the synthesis pipeline description: Section 5.3 describes passing discrete units to a 'pretrained Tacotron vocoder [10] to generate audio waveforms', whereas Tacotron is an acoustic model generating spectrograms, not a waveform vocoder. Details regarding vocoder training, speaker conditioning, and waveform generation are missing.

Ambiguities in the dataset description in Section 3 regarding speaker cohort size (the text alternates between 'participants were briefed' and 'with the subject articulating'), leaving it unclear whether the main 9-hour corpus comprises single-speaker or multi-speaker data.

strengths: Grounding SSL speech models in articulatory physiology: The paper provides a compelling empirical analysis demonstrating that self-supervised speech representations (particularly HuBERT layer 6) exhibit a strong linear relationship (r = 0.85) with EMG muscle power, offering a principled mechanistic rationale for why specific intermediate representations are optimal for speech resynthesis.

Realistic, alignment-free clinical setting: Unlike previous EMG-to-speech benchmarks that assume time-synchronized audio recordings, this method learns without frame-level alignment by leveraging TTS-derived discrete units and CTC loss, making it directly applicable to silent speech or voiceless patients.

Validation on clinical target population: In addition to a healthy speaker dataset, the method is successfully demonstrated on an individual with ALS performing silent articulation, showcasing practical feasibility under low-data regimes (~40 minutes of training).

Novel phoneme-guided consistency regularization: The proposed dual-head framework using a precomputed unit-to-phoneme mapping provides clear and statistically significant reductions in unit error rates (UER).

Valuable open-source community contributions: The authors release one of the largest public EMG-to-speech datasets (~9 hours general corpus, ALS corpus, and discrete gesture corpus) along with reproducible code and audio demonstrations.
weaknesses: Intelligibility and error rates: While MOS scores reflect good acoustic naturalness (3.79), the human-transcribed Word Error Rates remain quite high (62.55% on the general corpus, 50.82% on the ALS corpus), indicating that practical utility for seamless daily communication is still challenging.

Limited subject diversity for continuous speech: The speech experiments rely on data from a single healthy participant and a single ALS participant. The impact of cross-session non-stationarity (e.g., electrode re-placement, skin impedance changes) and cross-speaker transfer is left unaddressed.

Synthetic TTS target mismatch: Deriving HuBERT target units from Google TTS rather than natural paired speech solves the alignment issue but may introduce unnatural prosodic and temporal constraints that do not match the speaker's true articulatory dynamics.

strengths: Insightful representation probing: The paper provides compelling quantitative evidence that self-supervised speech (S3) representations (particularly intermediate layers such as layer 6 of HuBERT-base) have a strong linear mapping to orofacial muscle power (r = 0.85). This offers a principled mechanistic explanation for why intermediate HuBERT layers excel at articulatory and phonetic tasks.

Realistic clinical formulation: By formulating the EMG-to-speech problem without assuming time-aligned parallel audio (deriving target speech units from synthetic speech via text prompts and training with CTC), the approach is well-suited for aphonic patients or silent speech where time-synchronized acoustic audio is unavailable.

Valuable open dataset contribution: The authors contribute substantial public datasets, including ~9 hours of high-density EMG speech articulation from a healthy participant, ~1 hour of silent articulation from an ALS participant, and an articulatory gesture dataset across 12 subjects.

Principled phoneme-guided decoding: The proposed consistency regularization between frame-level phoneme posteriors and HuBERT unit posteriors via marginalization over a precomputed conditional distribution is elegant, articulatorily motivated, and yields statistically significant improvements in unit error rates.

Comprehensive experimental execution and transparency: The paper includes extensive details regarding electrode placement, architecture specifications, human perceptual evaluations (MOS and transcriber WER), and loss convergence analyses.
weaknesses: Participant diversity and longitudinal stability: The speech experiments rely on a single healthy individual (N=1) and a single ALS patient (N=1). The study does not evaluate across-session non-stationarities, electrode repositioning, or inter-speaker transfer, which are critical challenges for practical clinical deployment.

Moderate speech intelligibility: Word error rates from human listeners remain relatively high (62.55% on the general dataset and 50.82% on the small-vocabulary ALS dataset), showing that while the synthesized audio sounds speech-like (MOS 3.79), accurate linguistic transmission from unaligned surface EMG remains challenging.

Lack of direct benchmarking on standard datasets: While the authors justify why direct comparison to previous benchmarks like Gaddy & Klein (2020) is imperfect due to the unaligned setting, testing the proposed covariance features and phoneme-guided objective on existing open benchmarks would have provided a clearer reference point for the community.

strengths: Valuable resource contribution: The paper introduces and open-sources two substantial EMG speech datasets (approximately 9 hours with >6,800 unique words from a healthy participant, and 1 hour from an ALS participant) as well as an orofacial gesture dataset across 12 participants.

Insightful representation analysis: The linear probing analysis establishes a strong linear relationship (r = 0.85) between self-supervised speech representations (S3) and EMG power D(E), offering a principled articulatory explanation for why layer 6 of HuBERT-base performs well in downstream acoustic modeling.

Sound and clinically relevant formulation: Bypassing the assumption of time-aligned EMG-audio pairs during training by leveraging text-to-speech targets and CTC loss is well-motivated for assistive communication scenarios where patients cannot produce audible speech.

Methodological novelty: The phoneme-guided decoding framework, which regularizes discrete speech unit prediction using an articulatory consistency loss marginalized over unit-to-phoneme conditional distributions, demonstrates statistically significant improvements in unit error rate.

Comprehensive experimental reporting: The paper includes human transcription evaluations (WER and PER), mean opinion score (MOS) perceptual tests, training data scaling ablations, and extensive appendix documentation detailing electrode locations and model architectures.
weaknesses: High word error rates: The end-to-end word error rates remain relatively high (62.55% for the healthy participant and 50.82% for the ALS participant on a limited vocabulary), demonstrating that practical clinical utility is still limited.

Limited subject diversity for continuous speech: The continuous speech synthesis experiments are conducted on only a single healthy participant and a single ALS participant, leaving cross-subject generalization, day-to-day session variability, and electrode repositioning effects uncharacterized.

Absence of comparison on existing public benchmarks: While the unaligned gTTS target setting is justifiable, the lack of evaluation on existing standardized EMG-to-speech corpora (such as Gaddy & Klein 2020) makes it difficult to directly benchmark the proposed TDS encoder and covariance features against prior literature.

Divergence between perceptual quality (MOS) and intelligibility: The relatively high MOS (3.79) predominantly reflects the quality of the pretrained vocoder rather than the intelligibility of the synthesized linguistic content, given the high WER.
